events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners and renters will purchase consumer-grade laundry machines at higher price points because they view them as a convenience and status upgrade, not just a functional appliance. Who benefits: Homeowners, renters, and small landlords seeking convenience and modern aesthetics.. Why behaviour changes: Growing consumer demand for stylish, integrated home appliances and the convenience of self-service laundry reduce perceived utility of basic, utility-style appliances.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge premium prices for design, smart features, and brand positioning, and potentially license its technology to brands for consumer machines.. Assumptions: Consumers perceive self-service laundry as a modern amenity.; Price sensitivity for home buyers is lower than for professional buyers.; Electrolux's design credibility can be leveraged in consumer markets.. Predictions: Willingness-to-pay studies show consumers will pay at least 20% more for a designer self-service unit than a standard machine.; Consumer surveys indicate a desire for aesthetic integration with home decor.; Pilot sales show higher conversion rates for premium-priced units in pilot markets..

T2: Small businesses and rental properties will adopt consumer-grade laundry machines because they need reliable, low-cost solutions for guest laundry and staff facilities, and existing professional machines are too expensive or difficult to service. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, campsites, marinas, and rental property owners with limited budgets.. Why behaviour changes: High turnover of guest laundry and staff facilities makes it cheaper to replace machines than to upgrade, and consumers prefer machines that are easy to maintain and repair.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell lower-priced, easier-to-service units through retail and wholesale channels, and potentially offer service contracts to reduce downtime.. Assumptions: Small businesses have limited capital for new equipment.; Current professional machines are difficult to repair or replace.; Consumers prioritize ease of maintenance over brand prestige.. Predictions: Small business surveys show higher purchase intent for machines priced under $2,000 compared to professional-grade units.; Pilot sales in rental properties show higher adoption rates for machines with modular designs.; Customer satisfaction surveys highlight ease of repair as a key purchase driver..

Test "Premium vs. Value Messaging Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small business owners/rental property managers, recruited via panel to match demographics.. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) for a self-service laundry unit described with either premium design features (status upgrade) or cost-ease-of-maintain features (small business). Secondary measure: stated purchase intent (1‑10).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher WTP for premium-priced units (e.g., €1,500‑€2,000) than small businesses will show higher WTP for value-priced units (e.g., €1,000‑€1,500).; T2: Small businesses will show higher WTP for value-priced units (e.g., €1,000‑€1,500) than homeowners will show higher WTP for premium-priced units.. Decision rule: If homeowners’ average WTP for premium units exceeds small businesses’ average WTP for value units by at least €500, proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If small businesses’ average WTP for value units exceeds homeowners’ average WTP for premium units by at least €500, develop a value‑focused small‑business proposition. If both thresholds are met, pursue both propositions; otherwise, no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines (Alliance Laundry Holdings) and a self-service format capability (Electrolux), but no direct proof of premium pricing or status motivation. Run the proposed premium‑vs‑value messaging pilot to test willingness to pay before investing. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivation, pricing, or small business demand. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial-quality home machines (Alliance Laundry Holdings) and a self-service format capability (Electrolux), but no direct proof of premium pricing or status motivation. Run the proposed premium-vs-value messaging pilot to test willingness to pay before investing. Target customer: Homeowners and renters seeking convenience and modern aesthetics, and small businesses with limited budgets for guest laundry and staff facilities.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that combines professional-grade performance with design, smart features, and ease of use, enabling homeowners to run their own laundry and small businesses to provide reliable, low-cost guest laundry.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 8‑week, €18,000 premium-vs-value messaging pilot with 500 respondents to measure willingness to pay for premium‑priced units versus value‑priced units.. Uncertainty: The size of the premium price premium homeowners will pay and whether small businesses will adopt at lower price points remain uncertain. Evidence of actual purchase intent and market share is lacking.. Would change if: If the pilot shows homeowners’ average willingness to pay for premium units exceeds small businesses’ average willingness to pay for value units by at least €500, we would proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition.; If small businesses show higher willingness to pay for value units, we would develop a value‑focused small‑business proposition.; If neither threshold is met, we would maintain the current professional‑only focus.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

T1: Homeowners and renters increasingly view laundry as a convenience service, not a household chore, and will pay for self-service solutions that reduce wait times and effort. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who lack time or space for a traditional laundry room.. Why behaviour changes: Growing urbanization and time constraints make self-service laundry attractive; consumers prioritize convenience over cost.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling compact, consumer-focused machines through retail and wholesale channels, earning premium prices for convenience and reliability.. Assumptions: Consumer willingness to pay for self-service laundry is higher than for traditional machines.; Retail and wholesale distribution can reach target consumers effectively.; Electrolux can produce machines that meet consumer expectations for compact size and performance.. Predictions: In a test market, consumers will choose a compact self-service machine over a standard professional model when price is comparable.; Sales of compact consumer machines will increase in regions with high homeownership rates.; Consumers will report higher satisfaction with reduced wait times compared to traditional laundry..

T2: Small businesses and hospitality operators increasingly adopt self-service laundry to reduce labor costs and improve operational efficiency, and will invest in consumer-focused machines that offer scalability and lower maintenance. Who benefits: Small hotels, gyms, campsites, and other small businesses with limited laundry space and labor.. Why behaviour changes: Economic pressure to lower labor costs and improve ROI drives businesses to automate laundry processes; self-service reduces dependency on staff.. How value is captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling compact, scalable machines through wholesale and retail channels, offering financing and maintenance services to small businesses.. Assumptions: Small businesses are willing to invest in self-service laundry to reduce long-term costs.; Wholesale distribution can reach small businesses effectively.; Electrolux can produce machines that meet small business performance and durability requirements.. Predictions: In a test market, small businesses will choose a compact self-service machine over a standard professional model when cost per unit is comparable.; Adoption rates will be higher in regions with a high concentration of small hotels and gyms.; Businesses will report higher ROI from reduced labor and maintenance costs compared to traditional machines..

Test "Consumer vs Business Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small business owners (hotels, gyms, campsites). Recruit via social media and industry forums.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) for a compact self-service machine and intent to purchase based on messaging (convenience vs cost efficiency).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher WTP and purchase intent when messaging emphasizes convenience and reduced wait times.; T2: Small businesses will show higher WTP and purchase intent when messaging emphasizes cost savings and labor reduction.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the convenience message exceeds the average WTP for the cost-efficiency message by at least 10% among homeowners, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience. If the cost-efficiency message outperforms by at least 10% among small businesses, develop a consumer proposition focused on cost savings. If both thresholds are met, pursue both propositions.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, emphasizing convenience and reduced wait times. Begin with a limited pilot in high-homeownership regions to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address T1, as it tests the effect of durability and repairability messaging on purchase reservations, not consumer demand for convenience. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, emphasizing convenience and reduced wait times. Begin with a limited pilot in high-homeownership regions to test demand and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters in urban and suburban areas with limited laundry space and time.. Value proposition: Compact, self-service laundry machines that deliver professional-grade performance with a focus on convenience, reducing wait times and effort for daily use.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Business Messaging Test (8 weeks, €15,000) to validate willingness to pay for convenience messaging among homeowners and cost-efficiency messaging among small businesses.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for convenience and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. Evidence shows residential demand exists but does not confirm premium pricing or purchase intent.. Would change if: If the test shows small businesses prefer cost-efficiency messaging and higher WTP for cost savings, the recommendation would shift to a consumer proposition focused on small businesses.; If homeowners show no premium willingness to pay or low purchase intent, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

How value is captured: RATIONAL can charge a monthly subscription for recipe updates, smart features, and support, generating recurring revenue while leveraging its existing combi-steamer technology.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay for smart and subscription services.; Smart features are perceived as a significant advantage over traditional ovens.; Subscription model can be scaled without eroding brand loyalty.. T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, design‑focused appliance that signals status and quality, because they view cooking as a lifestyle and are willing to pay for brand prestige. Who benefits: Affluent home cooks who use cooking as a status symbol and are willing to invest in high‑end appliances.. Why behaviour changes: Design, brand prestige, and the perception of quality create a willingness to pay a premium price for a product that is seen as a status item.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can command higher price points, sell through premium retail channels, and capture value through limited‑edition designs and brand storytelling.. T3: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a health‑focused, low‑impact cooking solution that emphasizes steam‑based, nutrient‑retaining meals, because they seek healthier alternatives to traditional cooking. Who benefits: Health‑conscious home cooks who prioritize nutrient retention and low‑impact cooking.. Why behaviour changes: Health messaging and the perception of steam‑based cooking as a healthier option create a willingness to switch from traditional ovens.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can position the appliance as a health‑focused product, command higher price points, and sell through health‑focused retail channels, capturing value through premium positioning and brand association with wellness.. Assumptions: Health‑conscious consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product marketed as low‑impact.; Steam‑based cooking is perceived as a healthier cooking method compared to traditional methods.; Health messaging can be sustained without eroding market share in the mass market.. Predictions: Surveyed home cooks will rank health and low‑impact attributes higher than functionality when choosing a combi‑steamer.; Health‑focused models will show higher average transaction value than standard‑priced models.; Marketing health messaging will increase purchase intent among health‑conscious consumers..

Test "Smart vs Premium vs Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2; T3. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: Smart Group (smart features and subscription messaging), Premium Group (design and brand prestige messaging), Health Group (health and low-impact messaging). Each group sees a product description of a differentiated combi-steamer and is asked to indicate willingness to pay a fixed price (e.g., €1,200) and to choose a purchase channel (online, retail).. Sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three groups (100 per group).. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy). 3) Channel preference (online vs retail).. Predictions: T1: Smart Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent among home cooks, while Premium and Health Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.; T2: Premium Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent, while Smart and Health Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.; T3: Health Group will show the highest WTP and purchase intent, while Smart and Premium Groups will show lower WTP and purchase intent.. Decision rule: If the Smart Group's average WTP is at least 20% higher than the Premium Group's and at least 15% higher than the Health Group's, we conclude that smart features drive adoption and recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition with smart and subscription capabilities. If the Premium Group's average WTP is at least 20% higher than the Smart Group's and at least 15% higher than the Health Group's, we conclude that design and brand prestige drive adoption and recommend a premium positioning. If the Health Group's average WTP is at least 20% higher than the Smart Group's and at least 15% higher than the Premium Group's, we conclude that health messaging drives adoption and recommend a health-focused proposition. If none of these thresholds are met, we conclude insufficient evidence to favor any theory and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition that integrates smart features and a subscription model, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology to address home cooks’ demand for convenience and personalized cooking. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain; T3: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition that integrates smart features and a subscription model, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology to address home cooks’ demand for convenience and personalized cooking. Target customer: Affluent, tech‑savvy home cooks who value convenience, personalized cooking, and are willing to pay for smart and subscription services.. Value proposition: A smart, subscription‑enabled combi‑steamer that learns cooking preferences, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing support, offering a convenient, personalized cooking experience at a premium price point.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium vs Health Messaging Test (300 participants, 6‑week timeline, €20,000 budget) to measure willingness to pay, purchase intent, and channel preference across the three messaging groups.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether smart features, design and brand prestige, or health messaging drive adoption. Current evidence is limited to company assertions and market facts, and no direct consumer survey data is available.. Would change if: If the Smart Group shows a willingness to pay at least 20% higher than the Premium Group and at least 15% higher than the Health Group, we would shift focus to smart‑feature positioning.; If the Premium Group shows a willingness to pay at least 20% higher than the Smart Group and at least 15% higher than the Health Group, we would shift focus to premium positioning.; If the Health Group shows a willingness to pay at least 20% higher than the Smart Group and at least 15% higher than the Premium Group, we would shift focus to health‑focused positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain; T3: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

Test "Segmented Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) space‑constrained home segment (high density housing, small apartments), (2) small business/gym segment (limited staff, high volume), (3) neutral control. Each group sees a product description of a compact consumer‑grade machine (T1) or a durable consumer‑grade machine (T2). The survey measures willingness to pay (WTP) and intent to purchase on a 7‑point scale.. Sample: 300 respondents: 100 per segment, recruited via online panels to match demographic distribution of target segments.. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (1‑7) for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Group 1 will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than groups 2 and 3, indicating demand for compact consumer machines.; T2: Group 2 will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than groups 1 and 3, indicating demand for durable consumer machines.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the space‑constrained segment (Group 1) exceeds the average WTP for the small business/gym segment (Group 2) by at least 1.5 points on the 7‑point scale, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If the small business/gym segment (Group 2) exceeds Group 1 by at least 1.5 points, develop a proposition for small businesses. If neither segment exceeds the other by the threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential demand for commercial‑quality home machines, but it does not prove space constraints are the primary driver or that homeowners are willing to pay a premium. Conduct the proposed segmented messaging test to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

It does not address whether space constraints drive demand for compact consumer machines, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed segmented messaging test to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent before committing resources. Target customer: Homeowners and renters in high‑density housing and small apartments who face space constraints and seek convenience.. Value proposition: Compact, consumer‑grade machines that fit small spaces, offering reliable performance and hands‑on control of laundry, sold through retail channels to justify premium pricing while staying below consumer appliance market share.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the segmented messaging test (300 respondents, three groups, 6 weeks, €15,000) to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for space‑constrained home segment versus small business/gym segment.. Uncertainty: The primary driver of demand (space constraints vs. other factors) and the willingness to pay a premium for compact consumer machines remain uncertain. Evidence is limited to company assertions and a simulated result measuring messaging,. Would change if: If the test shows the small business/gym segment (Group 2) exceeds the space‑constrained segment (Group 1) by at least 1.5 points, we would develop a proposition targeting small businesses.; If neither segment exceeds the other by the threshold, we would maintain the current focus on professional laundry and not expand into consumer markets.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..

Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability and plastic waste reduction messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, significantly higher than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, significantly higher than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If Premium Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Sustainability Condition mean < 5.5, recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a monthly fee for smart cooking automation.; The device can be integrated with existing smart home ecosystems.; Subscription model is feasible without significant hardware redesign.. Predictions: In a test offering a subscription-based combi-steamer, at least 30% of surveyed home cooks will sign up within 3 months.; Repeat purchase rate for subscription will be at least 15% within 12 months..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that offers superior cooking performance and durability, because they value professional-quality results and are willing to pay a premium for it. Why behaviour changes: They would switch from lower-cost consumer appliances to a device that delivers consistent, high-quality results, reducing the need for multiple cookware items and time spent troubleshooting.. Test "Subscription vs Premium Combi-Steamer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and purchase intent measurement.. Sample: 500 German home cooks (aged 25-55) recruited via a panel, stratified by cooking frequency (daily vs occasional).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary: open-ended reasons for preference.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent for the subscription-based combi-steamer within 3 months, and willingness to pay will be above EUR 150 for the subscription model.; T2: At least 25% will indicate purchase intent for the premium-combi-steamer within 3 months, and willingness to pay will be above EUR 200 for the premium model.. Decision rule: If subscription purchase intent >=30% AND subscription willingness to pay >=EUR 150, proceed with a subscription-based home-cook proposition. If premium purchase intent >=25% AND premium willingness to pay >=EUR 200, proceed with a premium-combi-steamer proposition. If neither condition is met, maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions (premium messaging or sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than sustainability messaging.; T2: Sustainability messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 1.5 points higher than for sustainability messaging, conclude that premium positioning drives higher demand and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on taste and purity. If sustainability messaging is higher, recommend a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is below 1.5 points, indicate insufficient evidence to recommend a differentiated proposition and suggest further market research.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium taste and purity, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for superior water quality. Use direct‑to‑consumer channels and premium branding to capture value. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes premium taste and purity, targeting health‑conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for superior water quality. Use direct‑to‑consumer channels and premium branding to capture value. Target customer: Health‑conscious consumers in Denmark and adjacent markets who currently purchase water purifiers and are willing to pay a premium for perceived taste and purity.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced home water purifier that delivers superior taste and purity through Aquaporin’s biomimetic membranes, positioned as a lifestyle health product rather than a necessity.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test (300 participants, 4 weeks, €2,000) to measure purchase intent differences. If premium messaging yields at least a 1.5‑point higher score, proceed to develop the differentiated offer. Uncertainty: The size of the premium‑priced segment and actual willingness to pay remain uncertain. Evidence from the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows sustainability messaging yields a higher purchase intent score than premium messaging, we would shift focus to an eco‑friendly proposition.; If neither messaging condition meets the 1.5‑point threshold, we would recommend further market research before committing to a differentiated product.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Electrolux Professional Group develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing professional laundry offering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Homeowners and renters increasingly view laundry as a convenience service, not a household chore, and will pay for reliable, space‑saving solutions that can be operated by themselves. If Electron‑x can demonstrate a consumer proposition that meets this demand, it can capture premium pricing and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who need reliable laundry solutions and are willing to pay for convenience and performance.. Why behaviour changes: The shift from manual laundry to self‑service convenience drives demand for machines that are easy to operate, require minimal supervision, and fit small spaces.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell differentiated consumer models at premium prices through retail channels, leveraging its professional reputation to build trust and capture higher margins.. Assumptions: Consumer willingness to pay for a self‑service laundry solution exists and is measurable.; Electrolux can produce a consumer‑grade product that meets performance expectations.; Retail distribution channels are accessible to reach target consumers.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade self‑service machine to a sample of homeowners, at least 30% will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher among renters and first‑time buyers compared to homeowners with existing laundry solutions..

T2: Small businesses and professional users (e.g., gyms, marinas, campsites) face space constraints and need reliable, high‑cycle equipment that can be operated by staff or guests. If Electron‑x can offer a consumer‑grade product that meets these professional‑grade requirements, it can capture a new segment with higher volume and lower per‑unit cost. Who benefits: Small businesses and professional users with limited space who need durable, high‑cycle laundry equipment.. Why behaviour changes: These users prioritize reliability and performance over cost, and are willing to purchase equipment that can be operated by non‑experts.. How value is captured: Electrolux can sell consumer‑grade models through retail and wholesale channels, leveraging its professional reputation to build trust and achieve economies of scale.. Assumptions: Small businesses and professional users are willing to invest in durable, high‑cycle equipment.; Electrolux can produce a consumer‑grade product that meets professional performance standards.; Retail and wholesale channels are accessible to reach these segments.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑grade high‑cycle machine to a sample of small businesses, at least 25% will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Purchase intent will be higher among businesses with existing manual laundry solutions compared to those without..

Test "Consumer vs Professional Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a consumer‑grade self‑service machine description (focusing on convenience, space‑saving, and self‑operation) or a professional‑grade high‑cycle machine description (focusing on durability, reliability, and staff‑operation). Participants are recruited from homeowners (n . Sample: 300 participants: 150 homeowners (renters and first‑time buyers) and 150 small‑business professionals (gyms, marinas, campsites). Randomly assigned to either exposure group.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7‑point Likert scale (1‑not likely, 7‑very likely) and binary intent to purchase within 12 weeks.. Predictions: T1: Homeowners exposed to consumer‑grade description will show higher average intent than professionals exposed to professional‑grade description, and both groups will be above 5 on the intent scale.; T2: Professionals exposed to professional‑grade description will show higher average intent than homeowners exposed to consumer‑grade description, and both groups will be above 5 on the intent scale.. Decision rule: If the average intent for the exposed group is at least 5.5 points higher than the other group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for that segment. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 0.5 points, conduct a larger pilot test before committing.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters who value convenience, space‑saving, and self‑operation. Begin with a limited pilot test (e.g., a retail partnership or online offering) to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address T1, as it tests the effect of durability and repairability versus performance and price in a recruited population, not homeowner willingness to pay for a self-service proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters who value convenience, space‑saving, and self‑operation. Begin with a limited pilot test (e.g., a retail partnership or online offering) to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters who need reliable laundry solutions and are willing to pay for convenience and performance.. Value proposition: A consumer‑grade self‑service laundry machine that is easy to operate, fits small spaces, and offers professional‑grade reliability, positioned as a premium convenience product.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Professional Intent Test (or a larger pilot) to measure purchase intent and validate demand before committing to full development.. Uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a self‑service proposition is uncertain; the test will determine whether demand is sufficient to justify investment.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 5% or the difference between exposure groups is less than 1.5 points, we would abandon the differentiated consumer proposition and focus on the professional segment.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for premium self‑service laundry, we would reconsider scaling the consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions (premium messaging or sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than sustainability messaging.; T2: Sustainability messaging will yield a higher average purchase intent score than premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 1.5 points higher than for sustainability messaging, proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, proceed with a sustainability‑focused differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 0.5 points, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.; Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.; Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).; 2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.; 4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).; 5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition..

T1: Consumers will adopt self-service laundry solutions if they perceive higher convenience and lower wait times, because busy households value time savings. Who benefits: Households with limited time and those in multi-family buildings or student housing.. Why behaviour changes: Self-service machines eliminate the need to schedule a machine, reduce dependency on a service provider, and allow independent operation, making laundry accessible and convenient.. How value is captured: Electrolux can charge a premium for self-service units and sell additional consumables and accessories, capturing value through higher unit prices and recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers value convenience and are willing to pay a premium for self-service.; Electrolux can produce and distribute self-service units efficiently at scale.; Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer-operated machines.. Predictions: In a test market, households will choose a self-service unit over a traditional machine when convenience is emphasized.; Willingness to pay for a self-service unit will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable machine.; Adoption rates among households with limited time will be higher than among households with more time..

T2: Consumers will adopt self-service laundry solutions if they perceive higher cost savings and lower long-term ownership costs, because they seek to reduce recurring service and maintenance expenses. Who benefits: Households and small businesses that currently rely on professional laundry services or have high laundry costs.. Why behaviour changes: Self-service machines eliminate the need for a service provider, reduce water and energy consumption, and lower the frequency of repairs and consumables, making them financially attractive.. How value is captured: Electrolux can offer self-service units at a lower upfront cost than traditional machines and capture value through higher volume sales and reduced service margins.. Assumptions: Consumers are price-sensitive and will choose the lowest operational cost option.; Electrolux can produce self-service units at a cost-effective scale.; Regulatory standards allow consumer-operated machines to meet safety and performance requirements.. Predictions: In a test market, households will choose a self-service unit when cost savings are highlighted.; Willingness to pay for a self-service unit will be at least 15% lower than for a comparable machine.; Adoption rates among cost-conscious households will be higher than among convenience-focused households..

Test "Self-service vs machine choice test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: convenience condition (emphasizes time savings and self-service ease) or cost condition (emphasizes lower long-term ownership costs). They view a product description of a self-service unit and a comparable machine, and indicate which they would choose and the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two conditions (200 per condition).. Measure: Primary measure: choice of self-service unit vs machine. Secondary measure: maximum price willingness to pay for the chosen option.. Predictions: T1: In the convenience condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the cost condition.; T2: In the cost condition, participants will choose the self-service unit at a rate at least 15% higher than in the convenience condition.. Decision rule: If the difference in choice rates between the two conditions is at least 15 percentage points, we conclude that the corresponding theory is supported. If the difference is less than 15 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported. If the difference is inconclusive, we recommend further testing.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and self-service ease, targeting households with limited time and multi-family buildings. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test consumer willingness to pay a premium for self-service units. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability-and-repairability versus performance-and-price descriptions among a recruited population of household washing-machine buyers. It does not address consumer preference for convenience versus cost savings, so it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-EPRO-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes convenience and self-service ease, targeting households with limited time and multi-family buildings. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test consumer willingness to pay a premium for self-service units. Target customer: Households with limited time and those in multi-family buildings or student housing.. Value proposition: A self-service laundry unit that eliminates scheduling, reduces dependency on service providers, and allows independent operation, offering time savings and convenience.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 6‑week online survey test (400 participants, two conditions) to measure choice rates and price willingness. If the convenience condition shows a ≥ 15 percentage‑point advantage, proceed to develop a pilot product and pilot. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company assertions and one simulated result; no independent study directly measures consumer preference for convenience versus cost savings. The pilot will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows the cost condition wins by ≥ 15 percentage‑points, we would shift focus to a cost‑saving proposition.; If the pilot shows no significant difference between conditions, we would recommend further market research before committing to a full product launch.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified home barista consumers (regular coffee at home) and 250 non-home barista consumers (occasional coffee). Recruit via coffee forums and social media.. Measure: 1) WTP for a differentiated consumer product (e.g., compact espresso machine) at a premium price (e.g., 20% above standard professional price). 2) Intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2). 3) Primary reason for purchase (lifestyle vs functional).. Predictions: T1: Home barista consumers will show higher WTP and purchase intent than non-home barista consumers, and the primary reason will be lifestyle.; T2: Both groups will show similar WTP and purchase intent, with no significant difference, indicating the consumer market is not a large driver of Simonelli's revenue.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the differentiated product among home barista consumers is at least 20% higher than among non-home barista consumers, and purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 10% and purchase intent is not significantly higher, maintain the current portfolio.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista) with a premium, lifestyle-focused product, but first validate demand through a low-cost test before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista) with a premium, lifestyle-focused product, but first validate demand through a low-cost test before committing resources. Target customer: Home barista consumers who regularly prepare coffee at home and value quality and lifestyle.. Value proposition: A compact, premium espresso machine positioned as a lifestyle essential, offering superior taste, convenience, and brand prestige, with potential for higher margins and brand loyalty.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Preference Test (500 respondents, €20,000, 12 weeks) to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for a differentiated product.. Uncertainty: The size and profitability of the home barista market remain uncertain; Simonelli's current consumer sales are not publicly disclosed, and the decline in consumer business segments is a red flag.. Would change if: If the test shows a willingness-to-pay difference of less than 10% or purchase intent not significantly higher, we would maintain the current portfolio and not pursue a differentiated consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows the home barista market is growing rapidly and Simonelli's professional segments are not profitable, we would reconsider the investment.; If Simonelli's consumer sales data were publicly available and showed strong growth, we would reassess the case for expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Not interested" to 7 "Very interested").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, while Sustainability Condition will yield a mean score ≤ 4.5.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a mean purchase intent score ≥ 5.5, while Premium Condition will yield a mean score ≤ 4.5.. Decision rule: If Premium Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Sustainability Condition mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T1 is supported. If Sustainability Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Premium Condition mean ≤ 4.5, conclude T2 is supported. If both conditions meet their respective thresholds, both theories are supported. If neither condition meets its threshold, conclude no evidence for either theory.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Test "Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing automation and recurring revenue; Group B sees a premium, professional‑grade combi-steamer description emphasizing durability and performance. Both groups are shown a product description and a willingness‑to‑pay price point (proposed at €1,500). Participants indicate intent to purchase and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness‑to‑pay (in euros).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the subscription‑based smart combi-steamer development. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the premium‑priced professional‑grade combi-steamer development. If neither condition is met, do not expand into either segment and maintain current B2B focus.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a full-scale development yet. The evidence shows RATIONAL is a commercial kitchen leader with strong B2B performance, but it does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Sustainability Condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Sustainability Condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

case.question: Should RATIONAL develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks, building on its commercial combi-steamer technology, or stay with professional kitchens? What evidence would justify either choice?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

T1: Home cooks adopt combi-steamers mainly for convenience and convenience savings, not for gourmet performance, so they will pay more for a branded home unit only if it is positioned as a premium, convenience-driven product. Who benefits: Rational AG benefits by charging a premium price and selling directly to consumers through its own retail channels.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers switch from traditional cooking to combi-steamers when a single device replaces multiple appliances, saving time and effort. If they perceive a product as high-end and convenient, they are willing to pay more.. How value is captured: Rational AG captures value by selling premium-priced home units through its own brand, retaining margin and building consumer loyalty.. Assumptions: Home cooks already own at least one traditional cooking appliance and are aware of combi-steamers.; A premium positioning can be achieved without compromising the device's performance for home use.; Consumers are willing to pay a higher price for convenience and brand reputation.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced home combi-steamer, purchase intent among home cooks will be higher than for a standard-combi-steamers.; Willingness to pay will be significantly higher for the premium-priced unit compared to a standard unit.; Surveyed home cooks will cite convenience and time-saving as primary purchase drivers..

T2: Home cooks adopt combi-steamers mainly for gourmet performance and professional-quality cooking, so they will pay more for a branded home unit only if it delivers superior cooking results compared to traditional methods. Who benefits: Rational AG benefits by positioning its home units as premium, high-performance appliances and charging a premium price for superior cooking outcomes.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers switch to combi-steamers when they perceive a device that can achieve professional-quality results, such as even cooking, precise temperature control, and reduced cooking time.. How value is captured: Rational AG captures value by selling premium-priced home units through its own brand, leveraging its reputation for professional-grade cooking and justifying higher margins.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to invest in a device that promises professional-quality cooking results.; The performance advantage of a combi-steamer is perceptible and can be communicated effectively to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that offers superior cooking outcomes.. Predictions: In a test offering a high-performance home combi-steamer, purchase intent among home cooks will be higher than for a standard unit.; Willingness to pay will be significantly higher for the high-performance unit compared to a standard unit.; Surveyed home cooks will cite gourmet performance and professional-quality cooking as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Convenience vs. Performance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have used traditional cooking appliances. They are shown two identical combi-steamers (same features, price, and brand) with different descriptions: one emphasizing convenience and time-saving (e.g., 'Replace multiple appliances with one device, save hours in the kitchen.'), and one emphasizing gourmet performance and professional-quality results (e.g., 'Achieve even cooking and precise temperature control like a professional chef.'). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the convenience-focused condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the performance-focused condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for the performance condition, proceed with a differentiated home-cook proposition emphasizing convenience. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, stay focused on professional kitchens. If both conditions show similar intent, conduct a follow-up survey to test price sensitivity.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price. Who benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.; Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.. Predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.. How value is captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.; Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.; Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.. Predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.; Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product..
