Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium taste and purity) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium taste and purity messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability messaging).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Premium Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Sustainability Condition.; T2: Sustainability Condition will yield a higher average purchase intent score than Premium Condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Premium Condition is at least 1.5 points higher than for Sustainability Condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on premium taste and purity. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and consider other alternatives.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Home barista demand is driven by social interaction and the desire for a third-place experience, not just the technical ability to brew espresso at home. Who benefits: Home baristas and coffee enthusiasts who value the social aspect of coffee culture.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers seek a coffee experience that mimics the café environment, which they cannot achieve with traditional home brewing.. How value is captured: Simonelli can capture value by positioning its machines as premium, social-coffee experiences and by offering accessories or services that enhance the social aspect (e.g., coffee pairing guides, community events).. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a machine that offers a social coffee experience.; The social aspect of coffee is a significant driver of purchase decisions for home baristas.; Simonelli can effectively communicate and deliver this social value to consumers.. Predictions: In a survey, home baristas will rank social interaction as the top reason for purchasing espresso equipment.; Willingness to pay for a machine that offers a social experience will be higher than for a standard home brewing machine.; Sales of premium, feature-rich machines will be driven by social positioning rather than technical specifications..

T2: Home barista demand is driven by the desire for convenience and ease of use, particularly for busy professionals who need quick, high-quality coffee without the hassle of manual brewing. Who benefits: Busy professionals and small office workers who need reliable, high-quality coffee without the time and effort of traditional espresso machines.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift to home brewing when they find a machine that simplifies the process, reduces preparation time, and delivers consistent results.. How value is captured: Simonelli can capture value by offering compact, user-friendly machines with simplified controls and automated features, and by providing maintenance services that reduce the hassle of ownership.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and ease of use over advanced features.; The time saved from simplified operation is a significant purchase driver.; Simonelli can design and market machines that meet these convenience needs effectively.. Predictions: In a survey, convenience and ease of use will be ranked among the top reasons for purchasing espresso equipment.; Consumers will be willing to pay more for a machine that reduces preparation time.; Sales of compact, feature-rich machines will be driven by convenience positioning rather than technical specifications..

Test "Home Barista Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: social positioning condition (emphasizing the third-place coffee experience) or convenience positioning condition (emphasizing quick, easy brewing). They are then shown a product description of a compact, feature-rich espresso machine and asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 participants, recruited from a panel of home baristas and coffee enthusiasts, balanced across the two conditions.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (on a 7-point scale) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the social positioning condition compared to the convenience condition.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the convenience positioning condition compared to the social positioning condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the social positioning condition exceeds the average WTP in the convenience positioning condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, we conclude that social interaction drives demand and support T1. If the average WTP in the convenience positioning condition exceeds the average WTP in the social positioning condition by at least 1.5 points, we conclude that convenience drives demand and support T2. If the difference is within 1.5 points or both conditions show similar WTP, we conclude the evidence is inconclusive and the theories remain open.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Test "Segmented Pilot Test: Residential vs Small Business" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct locations: a residential building (e.g., a multi‑family apartment complex) and a small gym or fitness center. In each location, place a compact self‑service unit at a visible, accessible spot. Track the following metrics: (1) trial adoption rate (number of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks); (2) purchase intent measured via a short survey asking about willingness to pay a premium price (e.g., 20% above comparable consumer units); and (3) wholesale sales data (if the unit is sold through a distributor, track units sold).. Sample: Residential pilot: 50 units placed in 10 buildings, targeting 2,000 residents. Small business pilot: 20 units placed in 10 gyms, targeting 2,000 gym members.. Measure: Trial adoption rate (percentage of units used by residents or gym members within 12 weeks) and purchase intent (percentage of surveyed residents or gym owners indicating intent to purchase at a premium price).. Predictions: T1: Residential pilot adoption rate ≥ 10% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed residents; small business pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed gym owners.; T2: Small business pilot adoption rate ≥ 15% and purchase intent ≥ 20% of surveyed gym owners; residential pilot adoption rate ≤ 10% and purchase intent ≤ 15% of surveyed residents.. Decision rule: If the residential pilot meets both adoption threshold (10%) and purchase intent threshold (20%), proceed to develop a differentiated residential proposition. If the small business pilot meets both thresholds, proceed to develop a differentiated small‑business proposition. If neither segment meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Differentiated Purifier Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium‑priced purifier messaging emphasizing taste and purity; Group B sees a sustainability‑focused purifier messaging emphasizing reduced plastic waste. Both groups see a standard‑priced purifier as a baseline. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not at all likely to 7‑extremely likely) and state their top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 400 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (200 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) and top reason for choosing the product.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B, and taste and purity will be the top reason for Group A.; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A, and sustainability will be the top reason for Group B.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), proceed to develop a premium‑priced differentiated proposition targeting taste and purity. If Group B’s average is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A (i.e., Group B’s average ≥ 5.5), proceed to develop a sustainability‑focused differentiated proposition targeting eco‑friendly attributes. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated proposition and continue focusing on current B2B membranes.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

Why behaviour changes: If the device is positioned as a robust, industrial‑grade combi‑steamer designed for commercial kitchens, these users will choose it over consumer‑grade alternatives because they prioritize durability and performance.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Test "Smart vs Premium Subscription Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel arms: Arm A offers a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer at a fixed price; Arm B offers a premium, high-performance combi-steamer at a fixed price. Participants are randomly assigned to one arm. Both arms include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question and a purchase intent question.. Sample: 500 adult home cooks (aged 25-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both arms.. Measure: 1) Percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the device at the given price. 2) Average WTP (in euros) for each arm. 3) Purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Predictions: T1: Arm A will show at least 30% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a subscription-based model. Arm B will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.; T2: Arm B will show at least 25% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a premium, high-performance model. Arm A will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.. Decision rule: If Arm A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a subscription-based home‑cook proposition. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

If neither threshold is met, maintain the current B2B focus.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Espresso Machines" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to either a lifestyle segment (focusing on personal coffee experience and premium price) or a remote work segment (focusing on home office convenience and compact design). Each participant views a product description of a Simonelli home machine and is asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and likelihood to purchase.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 from lifestyle segment and 250 from remote work segment, recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Average maximum price willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale) for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle segment will show higher average maximum price and purchase intent than remote work segment.; T2: Remote work segment will show higher average maximum price and purchase intent than lifestyle segment.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price in the lifestyle segment is at least 20% higher than in the remote work segment, and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 points in favor of lifestyle, then T1 is supported and a differentiated lifestyle proposition is recommended. If the remote work segment's average price is at least 20% higher than the lifestyle segment, and the purchase intent difference is at least 15 points in favor of remote work, then T2 is supported and a remote work‑focused proposition is recommended. If neither segment’s price is significantly higher than the other, and the purchase intent difference is less than 15 points, the evidence is inconclusive and no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a design-forward, premium-priced home barista machine with social-sharing features (e.g., Instagram-friendly design, connectivity). Group B sees a compact, easy-to-use machine with time-saving features (e.g., quick brewing, compact size). Both groups are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 300 adult consumers interested in coffee, recruited via an online panel. 150 per group to ensure statistical power.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and will cite social sharing as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and will cite convenience as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), conclude that lifestyle/social-sharing motivation drives demand and T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude convenience drives demand and T2 is more likely. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.; Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).; 2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).; 3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.; 4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).; 5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use..

T1: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue. Who benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving, automated cooking solutions.. Why behaviour changes: Smart features and subscription model reduce manual effort and provide ongoing content, making the appliance attractive for daily use.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can charge a monthly subscription for recipe access, software updates, and premium features, generating recurring revenue while leveraging its existing combi-steamer technology.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a recurring fee for smart cooking features.; The subscription model is feasible without significant additional hardware costs.; Competitors do not offer a comparable subscription-based model.. Predictions: A pilot offering a subscription-based combi-steamer will achieve at least 10% monthly subscription conversion among targeted home cooks.; Surveyed adopters will report higher satisfaction with automated cooking compared to traditional appliances..

T2: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a premium, high-performance appliance that emphasizes precision cooking and professional-grade results, because they value quality and performance. Who benefits: Home cooks who cook frequently and seek professional-quality results.. Why behaviour changes: Premium positioning and performance claims create a perception of superior cooking capability, motivating purchase despite higher price.. How value is captured: RATIONAL can command premium pricing and differentiate itself in a market where performance is a key purchase driver, leveraging its existing technology to justify higher margins.. Assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a premium for perceived superior performance.; The premium positioning can be effectively communicated without overwhelming the product.; Competitors do not offer comparable premium positioning.. Predictions: A premium-priced combi-steamer will achieve at least 15% higher average transaction value compared to a comparable low-priced model.; Surveyed adopters will cite performance and precision as the primary reason for purchasing..

Test "Subscription vs Premium Messaging Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a subscription-based combi-steamer description emphasizing automation, recurring revenue, and recipe access. Group B receives a premium-priced combi-steamer description emphasizing precision cooking, professional-grade results, and high performance. Both groups see the same product specifications and price point.. Sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a recurring subscription fee (EUR 9.99/month).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay the subscription fee than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay the premium price than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5), proceed with the subscription-based differentiated proposition. If the average purchase intent for Group B is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A (i.e., Group B average >= 5.5), proceed with the premium-priced differentiated proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand into either segment.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition targeting home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology and marketing it as a smart, automated cooking solution with recurring revenue. Conduct a limited pilot to test demand before full rollout. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

Recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition targeting home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi-steamer technology and marketing it as a smart, automated cooking solution with recurring revenue. Conduct a limited pilot to test demand before full rollout. Target customer: Home cooks who value convenience, automation, and recurring revenue for daily cooking.. Value proposition: A subscription-based combi-steamer that delivers recipe access, software updates, and automated cooking, providing ongoing value and recurring revenue while using RATIONAL’s proven combi-steamer technology.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 8‑week pilot with 500 home cooks, randomized between subscription and premium messaging, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay the subscription fee. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with the. Uncertainty: The willingness of home cooks to pay a recurring subscription fee for a combi-steamer is uncertain. The pilot will determine whether demand is sufficient to justify scaling the subscription model.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the subscription model below 5.5 (i.e., no significant difference from the premium group), we would abandon the subscription-based proposition and focus on the premium-priced model.; If the pilot shows strong demand for the premium-priced model with willingness to pay above €1,200, we would shift resources to developing a premium-priced differentiated proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.
